title: The Best Playlist
premise: When Elodie Reyes's senior essay prompt asks 'What sound do you refuse to forget?', she writes about the jukebox in her late grandmother's diner—the one playing a playlist her grandmother recorded for a man she wasn't supposed to love, a Black musician who left Bellhaven in 1968. The essay leaks, and suddenly Elodie is the public face of a fight to stop the diner's demolition by the highway expansion her own father, a county commissioner, is championing. As she uncovers the love story hidden in the playlist's song order, Elodie must choose between the careful, dutiful daughter she's always been and the girl willing to lose everything—including her father's approval—to be heard. In the end, she plays the full playlist at the county hearing, and the town, moved by the truth, votes to relocate and restore the diner instead of razing it.
about_author: U. M. Lockridge is a former small-town radio DJ who grew up above her family's roadside diner in the Carolina foothills. She writes stories about the things families bury and the songs that dig them up.

chapters.title: The Question on Page One
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Staring at the college essay prompt, Elodie drafts three safe answers about debate trophies, then deletes them all. At the diner her grandmother left her—now shuttered—she finds the old jukebox still plugged in, humming. Emotional beat: the first crack in twenty years of careful silence.

chapters.title: Forty-Six Songs, One Order
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Inside the jukebox she finds a handwritten tracklist in her grandmother's script: forty-six songs in a deliberate sequence, ending with an unsigned dedication. Her father mentions at dinner that the diner block is slated for demolition in June. Emotional beat: inheritance becomes urgent.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Digging through the diner's back office, she finds a 1967 photo of her grandmother laughing beside a young Black guitarist holding a guitar case stenciled 'R.C.' The town archive clerk, Mr. Okafor, goes quiet when she shows him. Emotional beat: wonder shadowed by the town's buried history.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Mr. Okafor's memories of Ray Charles 'R.C.' Dupree, the musician who played the diner every Saturday until he was run out of Bellhaven. Elodie learns her grandmother kept his playlist in the jukebox for fifty years. Emotional beat: love that outlasted exile.

chapters.title: Debate Club Rules
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She treats the demolition fight like a debate case, gathering petitions and preservation codes, but her father finds her name on the petition and forbids her from 'embarrassing this family.' First real argument of her life. Emotional beat: duty versus conviction, and duty losing.

chapters.title: The Leak
chapters.summary: Her best friend Theo's POV. Theo submits Elodie's essay to the school's literary magazine without asking; it spreads through town, and the diner becomes a symbol. Elodie is furious, then terrified, then strangely free. Emotional beat: visibility forced upon her, and discovering she doesn't hate it.

chapters.title: Side B
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She decodes the playlist's second half: each song marks a date—a meeting, a promise, the night R.C. left. The final track was never recorded; her grandmother left the slot empty for a duet that never happened. Emotional beat: grief for a love that duty broke.

chapters.title: Father, Commissioner, Man
chapters.summary: Father's POV. Commissioner Reyes reads his daughter's essay and recognizes his own mother's handwriting in the reproduced pages—the grandmother he never spoke about after she chose the diner over the family's respectability. He doubles down on the demolition to bury it. Emotional beat: inherited silence repeating itself.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At the county vote, public comment closes early until Elodie takes the floor—not with a debate case, but with the jukebox, playing the playlist aloud while she tells R.C. and her grandmother's story. The room weeps; her father cannot look at her. Emotional beat: climax—truth as testimony.

chapters.title: The Empty Slot
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The council votes to relocate and restore the diner as a heritage site. Her father, at the diner's reopening, quietly places a 45 rpm record in the empty slot—a duet recording R.C. mailed in 1969, returned unopened. Elodie plays it. Emotional beat: reconciliation, and a voice finally heard.
